title: Global Liquidity Peaks: The More Aggressively You Poured into AI in H1, the Sooner You Get Discounted
dek: A stock market rally needs fresh money to keep buying. Global liquidity is already showing signs of peaking, and the companies that most aggressively invested in AI in the first half are shifting from being rewarded to being discounted.
why: This episode ties US AI capex, Hong Kong IPO activity, and household balance sheets into a single capital chain, offering a macro framework that doesn't treat AI as a cure-all.
who: For investors tracking both US AI and China/Hong Kong asset allocation, and for primary market practitioners gauging the source and pace of hot money in 2025.
skip: The discussion of specific Hong Kong IPO cases can be skipped; the main thread resumes at 8:11 with the Nvidia liquidity experiment.

points.h: Low IPO break rate is not a good sign
points.body: Don't take the low IPO break rate in Hong Kong as a sign of market strength. In the first half of this year, the break rate was only in the teens, far below the roughly 50-50 normal level under a market-driven mechanism. That means the participants were mainly short-term speculative arbitrage funds, not long-term investors. Recently, the supply of new listings has decreased, and some IPO-related funds have had problems, but the two newly listed companies still broke their IPO prices, showing that temporary supply-side controls haven't solved the fundamental issue: Hong Kong also faces peaking liquidity.

points.h: The more aggressive the AI spending, the sooner the punishment
points.body: Market sentiment reversed within a quarter. Before Q1, the capital market rewarded aggression: the louder the AI capex talk, the higher the valuation. By the end of July, when half-year reports were released, any major internet company that had made aggressive capital expenditures in H1—especially those that burned through free cash flow—was discounted, and even Google wasn't spared. Q2 was the most FOMO-driven quarter across the supply chain; everyone rushed to spend before prices rose, and inventory still supported gross margins. By Q3, with inventory depleted and price increases hitting, the adverse factors will emerge together.

points.h: Nvidia is closer to Cisco in 2000
points.body: Nvidia's earnings look good, but its cash flow is changing. Before the dot-com bubble burst in 2000, Cisco introduced 'rent-to-own' financing for customers, recognizing future revenue as sales upfront. Nvidia is now also pushing rent-to-own. In its earnings, free cash flow fell by half quarter-over-quarter, and accounts receivable are far above historical levels—possibly partly related to the credit enhancement and payment structure from rent-to-own. So Nvidia may have reached a point where it needs more aggressive financial tactics to sustain market expectations, similar to Cisco's situation back then.

points.h: Primary market money comes from bullets fired three years ago
points.body: The answer lies in fund-raising timing. The money concentrated in AI and robotics from H2 2025 to H1 2026 mainly comes from funds raised at the market peak in 2020-2022. From 2023 to 2025, they barely invested, until they saw state capital placing bets when no one dared and making the most money—the stories of CXMT and YMTC, two large language models, and two major chip companies spurred market-based funds. The mentality is: copy the state's playbook. So this isn't a rational long-term increment; it's more like a delayed emotional release.

points.h: New property policy removes households from the financing chain
points.body: The key of recent property policy is not to rescue developers but to detach households from the old financing loop. In the past, buying off-plan housing meant households acted as financing targets in the investment-driven chain: paying first, receiving the property later. The policy pushes the chain toward marketization, so buyers get completed homes and only act as consumers, with risk reset to developers and financing institutions. The policy was introduced when prices were near the bottom to first stabilize the denominator of the asset side, avoiding panic during a decline. Japan post-1990s and China's coal and mining industry consolidation followed similar paths.

points.h: A slow bull is not a slogan; it's about chip structure
points.body: A slow bull isn't achieved by shouting; it's about layering market chips by duration: at the bottom are low-valuation, high-dividend blue chips held by insurers as long-term money that rarely trades; above that are public funds and index funds, functioning close to a price-stabilizing role; CSFC and Huijin adjust the index at a higher level; and at the top are retail investors, private funds, and active management money. New insurance regulations require liabilities and assets to match in duration, yield, and liquidity, institutionally ensuring long money invests long, medium money medium, and short money short—not allowing short-term household money to be invested in ten-year, low-liquidity assets.

points.h: Crises grow bigger with each bailout; at least one and a half bubbles
points.body: Since the dollar left gold in 1971, global central banks have increasingly relied on printing money to intervene in crises, acting faster each time. The quantitative easing after 2008 was supposed to be cleared during the rate-hiking cycle, but political intervention interrupted it, and then COVID hit in 2020, layering an even larger wave of money on top of an unshed bubble—today we have at least one and a half bubbles accumulated. Central bankers have learned to print even more money at the first sign of crisis, with the endogenous result of inflation, financial asset appreciation, and wealth inequality all intensifying simultaneously. As long as bubbles aren't allowed to clear, the world may face some form of prolonged stagflation.

quotes.text: The reason I say it's a bit precarious is that today the whole world is facing a liquidity peak.
The capital market still thinks whoever spends aggressively is great, but when half-year reports come out, it becomes: whoever was aggressive gets punished.
Perhaps Nvidia has also reached a point where, in a sense, it needs rent-to-own to drive revenue growth and meet capital market expectations.
Everyone sees that you can pull off this story, so they think, 'I can definitely pull off this story too'—psychologically, that's about it.
The so-called slow bull we always talk about isn't because it's inherently slow and bullish; on the basis of a slow bull, you first need to build a chip structure.
Before the last pile of bubbles had dissipated, an even bigger one was added—and it was added without hesitation.
